title: A Big Mistake I See Leaders Make: Either/Or Thinking
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership, 8.28.26
summary: Leadership writer Kurt Mueller uses a cross-functional scheduling standoff — one department needing deliverables Friday, another insisting on next week — to diagnose a common leadership error: treating disagreement as a zero-sum contest to be won rather than a signal to look for a tradeoff. He argues that the instinct to advocate harder works for solo decisions but backfires across organizational boundaries, where pushing to win a deadline argument can damage the working relationship needed for future handoffs. Mueller offers a reframing question — asking what the other side is actually trying to protect and what can be adjusted — along with a short worksheet for separating protected outcomes from negotiable ones. The piece closes with a real resolution in which the leader realized she needed only partial information by Friday, letting both sides get what mattered without either side 'winning.'
points: Diagnoses 'either/or thinking' — treating a cross-functional deadline conflict as a contest one side must win — as a common leadership mistake that damages relationships needed for future collaboration.
Distinguishes solo, yes/no decisions (where advocating hard works) from cross-functional disagreements, where the other party has legitimate competing stakeholders and no one has full authority.

Reframes the operative question from 'whose requirement wins' to 'what are they actually trying to protect, and what can we adjust,' opening options like partial delivery, substituted resources, or now-versus-later sequencing.
Provides a four-line 'Tradeoff Reframe' worksheet and a suggested script for separating must-protect outcomes from negotiable ones before a conversation.

Illustrates the approach with a resolved example: a leader who needed a Friday deadline discovered she only needed three pieces of information by then, letting the rest arrive Monday without anyone 'losing.'
quotes: That is where many perfectly reasonable leadership disagreements start going downhill.
The deadline may be real. But the either/or thinking usually is not the answer.
Cross-functional disagreements are different. You usually don't have authority over the other person, and they have legitimate stakeholders, deadlines, and resource limitations of their own.
Push harder, and you may win the argument but damaging the relationship you will need for the next ten handoffs.
Before negotiating anything away, identify the two or three deliverables that really cannot move. Those are the outcomes whose absence would materially affect stakeholder success.

In my earlier example, the leader discovered that she didn't actually need the entire deliverable Friday. She needed three pieces of information so another team could begin its work. The remaining material could arrive Monday.
You have stopped treating the other leader as the obstacle and started treating them as a partner in solving the constraint.
